claims.text: Corrosion resistance in steels used for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is enhanced when hydrogen can effectively diffuse out of the microstructure.
Pre-straining introduces additional dislocations and microstructural defects.
Pre-strain-associated defects act as hydrogen-trapping sites.
Un-prestrained steel releases nearly all absorbed hydrogen during prolonged air exposure.
Pre-strained steel retains substantially more hydrogen during air exposure than un-prestrained steel.
Hydrogen out-diffusion preserves the protective passive oxide film.
Hydrogen trapped by pre-strain degrades the protective oxide film.
Degradation of the oxide film promotes corrosion initiation.
Hydrogen exposure and pre-strain reduce the fracture energy of steel.
After charging and air exposure, un-prestrained specimens will have lower retained-hydrogen levels than pre-strained specimens.
Un-prestrained specimens will retain a more robust passive oxide film than pre-strained specimens.
Un-prestrained specimens will exhibit lower corrosion rates than pre-strained specimens.
Pre-strained, hydrogen-exposed specimens will have lower fracture energy than corresponding un-prestrained specimens.
Steel that is neither pre-strained nor hydrogen-charged should have a stable oxide layer, low hydrogen content, and predictable corrosion resistance.
The proposed mechanism should hold primarily for carbon steels and low-alloy steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power settings.
The mechanism may not apply to high-alloy stainless steels because their corrosion and passivation behavior is governed by different chemistry.
Hydrogen concentration, fracture energy, oxide-film integrity, and corrosion rate can be compared between pre-strained and un-prestrained specimens to test the mechanism.
Failure of pre-strained specimens to show higher hydrogen retention, oxide degradation, lower fracture energy, and increased corrosion would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes pre-strain as being applied simultaneously with hydrogen charging, whereas the experimental design describes specimens as being pre-strained before both groups undergo hydrogen charging.
